In 30 seconds

What it is
CertiVault issues certificates bound to their issuer by a SHA-256 fingerprint and an RSA-2048 signature, with the signing key’s fingerprint pinned outside the database and a QR code on each one. Anyone can check a certificate without an account.
What I did
I worked on CertiVault with Anjali Chandewar and Falguni Chaudhari and maintained the public repository.
What came of it
One explainable verdict for every check, a Docker setup and a Render deployment blueprint. There is no public demo yet.

By design

6verdicts

Valid, tampered, expired, revoked, superseded or invalid: exactly one per check.

01 — CertiVaultCase studyCh. 01 / 08

01 — Problem

Certificates circulate as editable PDFs and images, and recipients have no quick way to check them.

Blockchain approaches add fees and latency, and still cannot prove that a ledger identity belongs to a real institution. CertiVault uses plain, well-understood cryptography instead: a fingerprint to detect any change, a signature to show who issued it, and a pinned key to catch a swapped one.

Trust
Signatures and key pinning, not a blockchain.
Access
Anyone can verify, with no account.
Clarity
Exactly one verdict per check, in a fixed order, so it can be explained.
Security
The content security policy allows no inline scripts.
Stack
PHP 8.2 with no framework, MySQL or MariaDB in strict mode.

“A signature proves who issued a certificate, not that its content is true.”

From the project’s own stated limitations · README.md

03 — CertiVaultCase studyCh. 03 / 08

03 — Technical architecture

Two lanes: an institution issues, and anyone verifies without an account.

Fig. 4.3 · CertiVault architecture, full

Scroll sideways to follow the whole drawing.
  1. 1Institution. An approved issuer sends certificate data.
  2. 2Issuance service. Canonical JSON, then a SHA-256 fingerprint, then an RSA-2048 signature.
  3. 3MySQL. The record and its signature, in strict mode.
  4. 4Certificate PDF. Carries a QR code with its ID.
  5. 5Key pin. The signing key’s fingerprint, kept outside the database.
  6. 6Transparency log. Optional: an append-only Merkle log with signed checkpoints.
  7. 7Holder. Shares the PDF, the QR code or a link.
  8. 8Public verifier. Anyone, with no account.
  9. 9verify.php. Exists, revoked, superseded, hash match, key pin match, RSA verify, expired: in that order.
  10. 10Verdict. Exactly one of six, shown in words and shapes, never colour alone.
04 — CertiVaultCase studyCh. 04 / 08

04 — Key challenges and decisions

  1. D1

    Signatures and a pinned key, not a blockchain.

    It avoids a blockchain’s fees and latency, and answers “who issued this?” with a key tied to an approved institution.

    Trade-offKey pinning is trust-on-first-use, and a single operator runs the system.

  2. D2

    A fixed order of checks.

    The precedence among verdicts is fixed, so a certificate gets exactly one verdict, and the verifier can say which check decided it.

  3. D3

    Open verification.

    Anyone can verify, without an account, by QR code, ID or link.

  4. D4

    No inline scripts.

    The content security policy forbids them, so every script is an external file.

  5. D5

    A lookup that grew with the table.

    The project’s notes report that the rate limiter slowed down as its table grew, and that the lookup was found and fixed during development.

05 — CertiVaultCase studyCh. 05 / 08

05 — Implementation and technology

Plain PHP and MySQL, with the cryptography in the open.

Each certificate is fingerprinted with SHA-256 over its canonical fields and its file, and signed with RSA-2048. The signing key’s fingerprint is pinned outside the database, and each certificate carries a QR code. The repository ships a Docker setup, a Render deployment blueprint, and automated PHP and headless-browser test suites.

Server
PHP 8.2, no framework; MySQL or MariaDB in strict mode
Cryptography
SHA-256, RSA-2048 via OpenSSL, AES-256-GCM, HMAC-SHA-256, TOTP, bcrypt
Browser
Vanilla JavaScript, Web Crypto, html5-qrcode, pdf.js
Delivery
dompdf, PHPMailer, phpqrcode, Docker, a Render blueprint, GitHub Actions

06 — Issue, then verify: a walkthrough

Pick what happened to the certificate, or edit its title yourself, and watch the seven checks run in order.

The fingerprint is a real SHA-256, computed in your browser over the same fields the repository documents. The certificate is fictional, and the key and signature checks are simulated.

07 — CertiVaultCase studyCh. 07 / 08

07 — Evaluation, results and limitations

The repository has automated PHP and headless-browser test suites. No test counts or performance figures are shown here yet.

Limitations

  • A single operator runs the system.
  • Key pinning is trust-on-first-use.
  • A signature proves who issued a certificate, not that its content is true.
  • There is no public demo yet, and no screenshots on this page.
